rows.text: homecoursesoptions trading fundamentalswhat is an option? calls & puts explainedintermediate·lesson 1 of 5·8 min readwhat is an option? calls & puts explaineda stock option gives its buyer a contractual right; contract size, exercise style and settlement terms determine what that right involves.by anuga weerasinghepublished by tradehq, created by anuga weerasinghe. publisher background and editorial approach. no independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. quick answerwhat is an option? calls & puts explained?a stock option gives its buyer a contractual right; contract size, exercise style and settlement terms determine what that right involves. a standard unadjusted us equity option generally covers 100 shares; adjusted and other contracts can differ. at expiration, before costs, a purchased call has a net gain above strike + premium; a purchased put has a net gain below strike − premium. those levels are break-even prices.the core definitionthis lesson focuses on standard unadjusted us equity options, which generally cover 100 shares. a call gives its buyer a right to buy and a put a right to sell at the strike under the contract terms. american-style options can be exercised before expiry; european-style options have a different exercise schedule. adjusted contracts and cash-settled index options can have different deliverables. the writer takes the corresponding obligation. read the specific contract and occ risk disclosure rather than assume every option is identical.because one contract controls 100 shares, a call option quoted at $2.50 actually costs $250 to buy. that single number embeds four separate ideas: the direction you expect (up for calls, down for puts), how far you expect the move to go (the strike), how much time you're giving it (the expiration), and how much volatility the market currently prices in.why options exista share holder can buy a put to offset some losses below its strike during the option term, at the cost of its premium. a covered call adds premium income but limits upside and retains substantial share-price risk. these examples illustrate different payoffs; neither is a guaranteed return or a universally suitable position.a simple worked exampleimagine apple trades at $180 and you buy one 30-day $185 call for $3.00 ($300 total). three things can happen. if apple closes above $188 on expiration, you're profitable — the intrinsic value of the call exceeds what you paid. if it closes between $185 and $188 you're partially in-the-money but net negative. if it closes at or below $185, the call expires worthless and you lose the full $300 — but nothing more. these are hypothetical expiration payoffs before costs for the purchased option alone. exercise can create a stock position with separate funding and market risk. short options have different obligations, and an uncovered short call can have unlimited loss.what you can practise on tradehqtradehq supports spot instruments, including shares and etfs, with $100,000 virtual capital. it does not model option strikes, expirations or premiums. use this lesson's worked examples to calculate hypothetical contract payoffs on paper; buying an underlying share in the simulator is a different transaction from buying an option on it.options are contracts, not shares. you are trading a right that decays with time.(educational only — not financial advice. tradehq offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) key takeawaysa standard unadjusted us equity option generally covers 100 shares; adjusted and other contracts can differ.at expiration, before costs, a purchased call has a net gain above strike + premium; a purchased put has a net gain below strike − premium. those levels are break-even prices.a purchased option held without exercise can lose its premium plus costs; exercise can create a separate underlying position and obligations.options can be used for hedging and speculation; their risk depends on the position and contract.check your understandinganswer all 4 questions to complete this lesson.1. how many shares does one standard us equity option contract control?10501001,0002. what is the maximum loss for someone who buys (goes long) a single call option?unlimitedthe strike price × 100the premium paidthe stock price × 1003. a call option gives the buyer the right to:sell shares at the strike pricebuy shares at the strike priceshort the stockreceive dividends4. buying a protective put alongside shares is an example of:eliminating every costa guaranteed gainhedging downside exposureavoiding contract termssubmit & complete lessonanswer noteshow many shares does one standard us equity option contract control? options: 10; 50; 100; 1,000. correct answer: 100. why: a standard unadjusted us equity option generally covers 100 shares. adjusted deliverables and other option types differ.what is the maximum loss for someone who buys (goes long) a single call option? options: unlimited; the strike price × 100; the premium paid; the stock price × 100. correct answer: the premium paid. why: for the purchased option alone before exercise and costs, loss is limited to the premium. exercise can create a separate position.a call option gives the buyer the right to: options: sell shares at the strike price; buy shares at the strike price; short the stock; receive dividends. correct answer: buy shares at the strike price. why: call = right to buy. put = right to sell.buying a protective put alongside shares is an example of: options: eliminating every cost; a guaranteed gain; hedging downside exposure; avoiding contract terms. correct answer: hedging downside exposure. why: a put can offset some downside below its strike, but the premium, expiry and other terms matter.sources & further readingocc — characteristics and risks of standardized options oic — options basics cboe options institute the greeks — delta, gamma, theta & vega practise this lessonuse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and daily settlement are conceptual exercises: calculate their examples in a worksheet, because tradehq does not execute derivatives contracts. educational simulation only — not financial advice.options trading fundamentalsall courseseducational simulation only — not financial advice. virtual money; homecoursesoptions trading fundamentalsthe greeks — delta, gamma, theta & vegaintermediate·lesson 2 of 5·10 min readthe greeks — delta, gamma, theta & vegathe four greeks quantify how an option's price reacts to stock moves, volatility, and the passage of time.by anuga weerasinghepublished by tradehq, created by anuga weerasinghe. publisher background and editorial approach. no independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. quick answerthe greeks — delta, gamma, theta & vega?the four greeks quantify how an option's price reacts to stock moves, volatility, and the passage of time. delta estimates underlying-price sensitivity, not a guaranteed payoff or real-world event probability. gamma is often relatively large near the strike close to expiration; volatility and other model inputs also matter.why greeks mattergreeks are model-based sensitivities to inputs, holding other inputs fixed. delta describes underlying-price sensitivity; gamma describes a change in delta; theta describes time sensitivity; vega describes implied-volatility sensitivity. interest rates and dividends can also matter. finite market moves need not equal a first-order estimate, and different pricing models can produce different values.delta — directional exposurea delta of 0.50 per share describes an approximate $0.50 option-price change for a $1 underlying move, with other inputs held fixed. for a 100-share contract that is about $50, before gamma and other effects. some traders use delta as a rough probability shorthand, but it is not a calibrated real-world probability and need not match the model probability of finishing in the money.gamma — how fast delta changesgamma measures how delta changes as the underlying moves. it is often relatively large near the strike close to expiry, depending on volatility and other inputs. dealer hedging can affect demand, but a chart or open-interest figure alone does not establish dealer positions, required hedges or the cause of a price move.theta — the ticking clocktheta estimates an option value change as time passes under a model, holding other inputs fixed. state whether the quote is per share or per contract and whether a calendar or trading-day convention is used. purchased options commonly have negative theta, but realised profit also depends on price, volatility and costs. selling premium is not a guaranteed collection of that estimate.vega — volatility sensitivityvega estimates sensitivity to a one-percentage-point change in implied volatility, with other inputs held fixed. implied volatility can change around earnings, but it need not rise before every release or fall afterwards. a long option can lose despite a favorable underlying move if time decay and a volatility decline offset that move.every option position is really four separate bets: on direction, on the speed of that direction, on time, and on volatility.(educational only — not financial advice. tradehq offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) key takeawaysdelta estimates underlying-price sensitivity, not a guaranteed payoff or real-world event probability.gamma is often relatively large near the strike close to expiration; volatility and other model inputs also matter.theta is a model sensitivity; other price changes can offset or exceed it.vega measures volatility sensitivity; a change in implied volatility is a different quantity.check your understandinganswer all 4 questions to complete this lesson.1. what does theta measure?directional exposuretime decay per dayvolatility sensitivityinterest-rate risk2. in the lesson example, a 0.50 delta and a $1 underlying rise imply approximately what change per option share, before other effects?$0.10$0.30$0.50$0.903. any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. quick answerdefined-risk spreads — verticals & iron condors?vertical spreads and iron condors illustrate bounded expiration payoffs, with execution and assignment risks to consider. certain spreads have bounded theoretical expiration payoffs when their legs remain intact. the example's $200 debit and $300 maximum gain exclude costs and additional stock exposure.comparing expiration payoffsa spread combines long and short options. certain vertical spreads have bounded theoretical payoffs at expiration, unlike an uncovered short call. that comparison does not make spreads universally safe or suitable for beginners. tradehq does not execute options spreads; the examples below are worksheet exercises.bull call spread — a hypothetical exampleassume one standard 100-share contract per leg, the same expiration, a $180 long call costing $4 per share and a $185 short call receiving $2. the net debit is $200. with both legs resolved as the expiration payoff assumes, the maximum loss is $200 and the maximum gain is ($185 - $180) × 100 - $200 = $300, before costs. at a $182 expiration price, the $200 intrinsic value offsets the debit for gross break-even. these selected quotes are arithmetic inputs, not current apple prices or a recommended trade.iron condor — another payoff structurea short iron condor combines a put credit spread below and a call credit spread above the underlying price. with all four legs intact, its expiration payoff has a maximum gain equal to the net credit when the price lies between the short strikes. movement beyond the range can produce a loss. time decay and implied volatility affect its value before expiration; this structure is an example for comparison rather than a preferred trade.a hypothetical sizing worksheetfor arithmetic practice, suppose a worksheet assigns 1-2% of a hypothetical $100,000 account to a trade's planned loss budget: that is $1,000-$2,000. these percentages are assumptions, not an institutional standard or a recommendation for a real account. repeated losses reduce equity, and correlated positions can lose together. the percentage alone does not establish how many trades an account can withstand.what the payoff diagram leaves outcosts and poor fills can change realised results. american-style short options can be assigned before expiration. exercise or assignment of only one leg can leave stock exposure, particularly near a strike at expiration. a bounded payoff diagram assumes the legs are maintained and resolved together; it is not a guarantee about every account outcome. closing a spread can reduce remaining expiration exposure but adds execution costs and cannot undo earlier assignment.worksheet comparisoncalculate the bull call example at expiration prices of $175, $182 and $190. then add an assumed $8 in total costs: the gross outcomes of -$200, $0 and +$300 become -$208, -$8 and +$292. separately describe what could happen if the short leg were assigned and the stock position remained open. keep that exposure separate from the intact-spread payoff.(educational only — not financial advice. tradehq offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) key takeawayscertain spreads have bounded theoretical expiration payoffs when their legs remain intact.the example's $200 debit and $300 maximum gain exclude costs and additional stock exposure.an iron condor's range-based payoff does not make it a preferred or safe trade.tradehq supports spot simulation; options spreads are studied in worksheets.check your understandinganswer all 4 questions to complete this lesson.1. for the intact bull call example, maximum expiration loss before costs is:unlimitedthe width of the spreadthe $200 net debitthe strike price2. an intact short iron condor has its maximum gross expiration gain when the underlying:rallies sharply beyond the upper wingcrashes beyond the lower wingfinishes between the short strikesgoes to zero3. in the worksheet, 1-2% of a hypothetical $100,000 account equals:$50,000$25,000$1,000-$2,000$1004. why can an expiration payoff diagram understate account exposure?it guarantees a profitit includes all commissionsassignment of one leg can leave a stock positionspreads cannot losesubmit & complete lessonanswer notesfor the intact bull call example, maximum expiration loss before costs is: options: unlimited; the width of the spread; the $200 net debit; the strike price. correct answer: the $200 net debit. why: both calls expire worthless below $180, leaving the $200 debit as the gross loss. costs and separate stock exposure are excluded.an intact short iron condor has its maximum gross expiration gain when the underlying: options: rallies sharply beyond the upper wing; crashes beyond the lower wing; finishes between the short strikes; goes to zero. correct answer: finishes between the short strikes. why: the four options expire without intrinsic value between the short strikes, leaving the credit before costs.in the worksheet, 1-2% of a hypothetical $100,000 account equals: options: $50,000; $25,000; $1,000-$2,000; $100. correct answer: $1,000-$2,000. why: 100,000 × 0.01 to 0.02 = $1,000-$2,000. the percentages are illustrative assumptions, not a universal standard.why can an expiration payoff diagram understate account exposure? options: it guarantees a profit; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. quick answerimplied volatility & trading around earnings?implied volatility is a model-implied input derived from option prices, with limits as a forecast of realised volatility. iv is inferred from option prices under a model; it can differ from future realised volatility. iv rank contextualises today's iv against the last 12 months.what implied volatility actually isimplied volatility (iv) is the volatility figure that, plugged into an option pricing model, would produce the option's current market price. it is not a prediction any single person makes — it emerges from the aggregate bids and offers of every participant. changes can reflect expected uncertainty, demand for protection and risk premiums. iv is model-dependent and need not equal later realised volatility.iv rank vs iv percentilethe raw iv number is meaningless without context. iv rank compares today's iv to the highest and lowest reading of the last 12 months on a 0-100 scale. iv percentile tells you what fraction of the last year the stock traded below today's iv. neither an iv-rank threshold nor an iv-percentile threshold establishes a buy or sell rule. compare the chosen lookback, option expiry, price source and costs before interpreting either measure.the earnings trapimplied volatility often rises before earnings and can fall sharply afterwards. a trader can be directionally correct and still lose on a long option if the volatility drop and time decay outweigh the price move.comparing hypothetical earnings payoffsin a paper worksheet, compare hypothetical long-premium and defined-risk premium-selling structures around earnings to see how direction, implied volatility and the size of the actual move interact. tradehq does not price these structures. avoid treating volatility selling as inherently safer; short premium can carry substantial risk.practice loopfor a historical study, record dated option quotes and implied-volatility observations from an options-data source before and after an earnings announcement. keep the expiry, strike and data methodology consistent, and record price changes as well as volatility changes. tradehq does not supply an options chain or iv-rank data. a small sample can illustrate mechanisms without establishing a reliable trading edge.(educational only — not financial advice. tradehq offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) key takeawaysiv is inferred from option prices under a model; it can differ from future realised volatility.iv rank contextualises today's iv against the last 12 months.iv crush after earnings can turn a correct directional bet into a loss.elevated implied volatility changes the payoff profile of premium-selling strategies, but higher premiums also reflect higher expected uncertainty and risk.check your understandinganswer all 4 questions to complete this lesson.1. iv rank of 80 means:iv is at 80%iv is near a 12-month highiv is near a 12-month low80% of options are profitable2. why can a long option lose even if the price moves in the expected direction after earnings?because options never follow the underlyinga drop in implied volatility and time value can offset the directional gainbecause earnings cancel the contractbecause all options are illiquid3. what does a high iv rank tell you?a premium-selling trade is guaranteed to workcurrent implied volatility is high relative to its own recent rangethe stock must fallthe next move will be small4. implied volatility is:historical vol over 30 daysan exchange forecastthe volatility that makes model = market pricethe stock's betasubmit & complete lessonanswer notesiv rank of 80 means: options: iv is at 80%; iv is near a 12-month high; iv is near a 12-month low; 80% of options are profitable. correct answer: iv is near a 12-month high. why: iv rank normalises iv against the last year on a 0-100 scale.why can a long option lose even if the price moves in the expected direction after earnings? options: because options never follow the underlying; a drop in implied volatility and time value can offset the directional gain; because earnings cancel the contract; because all options are illiquid. correct answer: a drop in implied volatility and time value can offset the directional gain. why: option value depends on more than direction; implied volatility and time value can change sharply after earnings.what does a high iv rank tell you? options: a premium-selling trade is guaranteed to work; current implied volatility is high relative to its own recent range; the stock must fall; the next move will be small. correct answer: current implied volatility is high relative to its own recent range. why: iv rank is context about relative option pricing, not a standalone buy or sell signal.implied volatility is: options: historical vol over 30 days; an exchange forecast; the volatility that makes model = market price; the stock's beta. correct answer: the volatility that makes model = market price. why: iv is the vol input that reconciles a pricing model with the live option price.sources & further readingoic — vega and implied volatility sensitivity oic — iv rank and percentile definitions defined-risk spreads — verticals & iron condorsoptions risk management — sizing, rolling & cutting losses practise this lessonuse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and daily settlement are conceptual exercises: calculate their examples in a worksheet, because tradehq does not execute derivatives contracts. educational simulation only — not financial advice.options trading fundamentalsall courseseducational simulation only — not financial advice. virtual money; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. quick answeroptions risk management — sizing, rolling & cutting losses?options losses can be amplified by position size, leverage, volatility and time decay. this lesson measures those risks using hypothetical contract examples. use a predefined practice risk budget and record the effect on drawdown. model adverse scenarios for structures whose losses can exceed the premium collected.illustrative 1% budget for a defined-risk worksheetfor simulation, choose a small predefined risk budget before entering a position and compare how different limits affect drawdown. for example, 1% of a $100,000 practice account is $1,000. this is an educational parameter, not a universal real-money rule.testing a hypothetical loss multipliernaked puts and short strangles can create losses far larger than the premium collected. in a paper worksheet, model adverse moves explicitly and compare the resulting losses with a hypothetical risk budget rather than relying on one fixed multiplier. tradehq does not execute these option positions.rolling — extending, not doubling downrolling means closing an existing option and opening another with a different expiry and sometimes a different strike. a credit or debit alone does not determine whether the adjustment makes sense; compare the new maximum loss, break-even points, time remaining and total capital at risk in a worked example. rolling options is not supported by tradehq's order engine.when to cut a losspredefined exits can prevent open-ended decision-making, but no single percentage works for every option structure. in a worksheet with appropriate historical option prices, compare several hypothetical exit rules and record drawdown, average loss and opportunity cost. account for execution assumptions and costs; tradehq's spot simulator cannot perform this options backtest.journaling every tradefor each hypothetical options example, record the thesis, dated volatility inputs, contract size, possible loss, exit assumptions and calculated p&l in a separate worksheet. tradehq's journal records supported simulator trades; the simulator does not execute them.) key takeawaysuse a predefined practice risk budget and record the effect on drawdown.model adverse scenarios for structures whose losses can exceed the premium collected.evaluate a roll by its full risk profile, not only by whether it creates a credit or debit.test predefined exits in simulation rather than treating one threshold as universal.check your understandinganswer all 4 questions to complete this lesson.1. why define a risk budget before a simulated options trade?to guarantee profitto control the potential effect of one lossto predict volatilityto avoid all drawdowns2. what should be compared when evaluating a roll?only whether it creates a creditonly the new expirythe new risk, break-even points, cost and time remainingnothing — rolling is always better3. how can a hypothetical options exit rule be studied outside tradehq’s spot engine?assume one percentage always worksuse a separate options-data worksheet with explicit fills and costschange the rule after every lossignore position size4. why journal every trade?tax onlyreview recorded assumptions and mistakesrequired by regulatorsboosts win rate automaticallysubmit & complete lessonanswer noteswhy define a risk budget before a simulated options trade? options: to guarantee profit; to control the potential effect of one loss; to predict volatility; to avoid all drawdowns. correct answer: to control the potential effect of one loss. why: a predefined risk budget limits how much one trade can affect the practice account; there is no universal percentage that fits every trader or strategy.what should be compared when evaluating a roll? options: only whether it creates a credit; only the new expiry; the new risk, break-even points, cost and time remaining; nothing — rolling is always better. correct answer: the new risk, break-even points, cost and time remaining. why: a roll changes several dimensions of the position, so the full risk profile matters more than credit versus debit alone.how can a hypothetical options exit rule be studied outside tradehq’s spot engine? options: assume one percentage always works; a selected sample cannot validate future performance.why journal every trade? options: tax only; review recorded assumptions and mistakes; required by regulators; boosts win rate automatically. correct answer: review recorded assumptions and mistakes. why: a journal records assumptions and observed mistakes. it does not prove a statistical edge or predict future profits.sources & further readingocc — options risk disclosure oic — options basics implied volatility & trading around earningsback to track practise this lessonuse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and daily settlement are conceptual exercises: calculate their examples in a worksheet, because tradehq does not execute derivatives contracts. educational simulation only — not financial advice.options trading fundamentalsall courseseducational simulation only — not financial advice. virtual money; homecoursesfutures & derivativeswhat is a futures contract?intermediate·lesson 1 of 5·8 min readwhat is a futures contract?a futures contract is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a fixed quantity of an asset at a set price on a set future date.by anuga weerasinghepublished by tradehq, created by anuga weerasinghe. publisher background and editorial approach. no independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. quick answerwhat is a futures contract??a futures contract is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement to buy or sell a fixed quantity of an asset at a set price on a set future date. a futures contract is a standardised exchange agreement to transact a fixed asset at a future date. the clearing house manages counterparty risk through safeguards; it does not eliminate all risk.the core definitiona futures contract is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement with a specified underlying asset or reference, contract size and settlement date. settlement can involve physical delivery or a cash payment under the contract rules. the clearing house acts as central counterparty to cleared trades and uses margin, settlement and default safeguards to manage risk. clearing reduces counterparty exposure; it does not make default impossible or protect a position from market losses.contract specifications matterevery futures contract has a spec sheet: contract size, tick size, tick value, trading hours, delivery month, and settlement method (physical or cash). these details determine the exposure and settlement obligations. one e-mini s&p 500 contract represents $50 × the index — with the index at 5,000, a single contract has $250,000 of notional exposure.long and short positionsa participant can open a long futures position by buying or a short position by selling the contract. a short futures position does not require first borrowing the underlying asset as a short stock sale does. both directions remain subject to margin requirements, broker permissions and applicable exchange rules, including position limits. the contract's settlement obligations still matter; being able to sell first does not mean that trading is unrestricted.speculators and price discoveryhedgers use futures to offset exposure to price changes in another activity or holding. speculators accept price exposure in pursuit of a trading profit. for a hypothetical producer, a short futures position may offset some losses from a falling sale price; the hedge can be imperfect if the cash and futures prices move differently. these roles help explain why participants trade. this lesson does not assign a universal percentage of market volume to either group.(educational only — not financial advice. tradehq offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) key takeawaysa futures contract is a standardised exchange agreement to transact a fixed asset at a future date.the clearing house manages counterparty risk through safeguards; it does not eliminate all risk.both long and short futures positions remain subject to margin, permissions and exchange rules.every contract has a spec sheet — always read it.check your understandinganswer all 4 questions to complete this lesson.1. the central counterparty on a us futures exchange is:the buyerthe sellerthe exchange's clearing housethe broker2. notional value of one e-mini s&p at index 5,000 ≈$5,000$50,000$250,000$1,000,0003. which statement about opening a short futures position is correct?it removes margin requirementsit is exempt from exchange rulesit does not require borrowing the underlying asset firstit guarantees a maximum loss4. a producer uses a short futures position to offset falling sale prices. this is an example of:guaranteed profiteliminating default riskhedging price exposureavoiding all settlement obligationssubmit & complete lessonanswer notesthe central counterparty on a us futures exchange is: options: the buyer; the seller; the exchange's clearing house; the broker. correct answer: the exchange's clearing house. why: the clearing house novates every trade.notional value of one e-mini s&p at index 5,000 ≈ options: $5,000; $50,000; $250,000; $1,000,000. correct answer: $250,000. why: $50 × 5,000 = $250,000.which statement about opening a short futures position is correct? options: it removes margin requirements; it is exempt from exchange rules; it does not require borrowing the underlying asset first; it guarantees a maximum loss. correct answer: it does not require borrowing the underlying asset first. why: selling a futures contract creates short exposure, subject to margin and applicable trading rules.a producer uses a short futures position to offset falling sale prices. this is an example of: options: guaranteed profit; eliminating default risk; hedging price exposure; avoiding all settlement obligations. correct answer: hedging price exposure. why: the futures position can offset some price exposure, but a hedge need not remove every risk.sources & further readingcme — futures introduction and participant roles cme — introduction to futures cme — e-mini s&p 500 contract specifications cme — clearing safeguards cme — position limits overview margin & leverage in futures practise this lessonuse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and daily settlement are conceptual exercises: calculate their examples in a worksheet, because tradehq does not execute derivatives contracts. educational simulation only — not financial advice.futures & derivativesall courseseducational simulation only — not financial advice. virtual money; it does not eliminate all risk.the core definitiona futures contract is a standardised, exchange-traded agreement with a specified underlying asset or reference, contract size and settlement date. settlement can involve physical delivery or a cash payment under the contract rules. the clearing house acts as central counterparty to cleared trades and uses margin, settlement and default safeguards to manage risk. clearing reduces counterparty exposure; being able to sell first does not mean that trading is unrestricted.speculators and price discoveryhedgers use futures to offset exposure to price changes in another activity or holding. speculators accept price exposure in pursuit of a trading profit. for a hypothetical producer, a short futures position may offset some losses from a falling sale price; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. quick answercontango & backwardation — term structure explained?compare prices across delivery dates and study carrying costs, supply conditions and the assumptions behind rolling exposure. contango: later delivery trades above nearer delivery in the comparison; homecoursesfutures & derivativeshedging with futures — the original use caseintermediate·lesson 4 of 5·8 min readhedging with futures — the original use casehedging is one use of futures. airlines may hedge fuel, producers may hedge output, and funds may hedge equity beta.by anuga weerasinghepublished by tradehq, created by anuga weerasinghe. publisher background and editorial approach. no independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. quick answerhedging with futures — the original use case?hedging is one use of futures. airlines may hedge fuel, producers may hedge output, and funds may hedge equity beta. hedging uses a position to offset a specified exposure; it need not eliminate every risk. producers sell; consumers buy.the airline case studyhypothetical cross-hedge: an airline with future jet-fuel costs considers a crude-oil futures position. rising futures prices could offset part of a higher fuel bill, but jet fuel and crude oil are different products, the hedge quantity and delivery dates may not match, and margins can require cash before the fuel purchase. it is not a lock on the airline’s complete fuel cost.the farmer case studyhypothetical producer hedge: a farmer expecting to sell corn later takes a short futures position in a chosen contract month. a fall in the futures price could produce a gain offsetting part of a lower cash sale price. the final result also depends on local basis, quantity, crop yield, contract terms and costs. the futures entry price is not a guarantee of the final net farm receipt.portfolio hedging with equity index futuresin a hypothetical worksheet, $50 million divided by $250,000 of contract notional gives 200 contracts. that arithmetic assumes one-for-one exposure; actual hedge sizing also depends on portfolio beta, basis risk and contract specifications. it does not guarantee full neutralisation or establish trading volume.the hedge is never perfectbasis risk concerns changes in the relationship between the hedged exposure and the futures price. a hedge can reduce one exposure while introducing margin liquidity, execution and operational risks. its effectiveness depends on the products, quantities, dates and outcome being measured; neither complete protection nor a fixed amount of risk reduction follows from the label hedge.(educational only — not financial advice. tradehq offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) key takeawayshedging uses a position to offset a specified exposure; it need not eliminate every risk.producers sell; consumers buy.equity funds hedge beta by shorting index futures.basis changes, cash-flow needs and mismatched quantities can affect a hedge.check your understandinganswer all 4 questions to complete this lesson.1. which conceptual futures direction offsets some exposure to a falling wheat sale price?buy wheat futuressell wheat futuresbuy corn futuresbuy s&p2. which conceptual crude futures position gains if its futures price rises?sell crude futuresbuy crude futuresbuy s&pdo nothing3. basis risk is:exchange defaultfutures vs physical don't move perfectly togetherrate riskfx risk4. hedge $50m with $250k notional contracts →202005001,000submit & complete lessonanswer noteswhich conceptual futures direction offsets some exposure to a falling wheat sale price? options: buy wheat futures; sell wheat futures; buy corn futures; buy s&p. correct answer: sell wheat futures. why: a short wheat future can gain when its futures price falls, but basis, quantity and costs affect the combined result.which conceptual crude futures position gains if its futures price rises? options: sell crude futures; buy crude futures; buy s&p; do nothing. correct answer: buy crude futures. why: buying futures profits if crude rises.basis risk is: options: exchange default; futures vs physical don't move perfectly together; rate risk; fx risk. correct answer: futures vs physical don't move perfectly together. why: basis fluctuates.hedge $50m with $250k notional contracts → options: 20; 200; 500; 1,000. correct answer: 200. why: $50m / $250k = 200.sources & further readingcme — hedging cme — hedgers and futures mechanics contango & backwardation — term structure explainedmicro futures — contract size and risk practise this lessonuse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and daily settlement are conceptual exercises: calculate their examples in a worksheet, because tradehq does not execute derivatives contracts. educational simulation only — not financial advice.futures & derivativesall courseseducational simulation only — not financial advice. virtual money; the margin deposit is not the amount of exposure or a maximum loss.on the simulatortradehq's $100,000 practice account supports spot instruments. it does not model futures contracts, initial or maintenance margin, daily settlement, or margin calls. use a paper worksheet to calculate a hypothetical contract's daily p&l and margin balance; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. quick answerthe yield curve and recession-risk research?yield-curve inversion has historically been associated with elevated us recession risk, but timing varies and the signal is not a standalone forecast. the yield curve is normally upward-sloping. inversions have historically been associated with elevated recession risk, with timing that varies across cycles.what the yield curve isthe yield curve plots the yield on us treasury securities across maturities — from 3 months out to 30 years. in normal times it's upward-sloping: you get paid more for lending longer. when short-term yields exceed long-term yields, the curve is inverted.why inversion signals recessionan inverted curve can reflect expectations for slower growth, lower future policy rates, or changing term premia. historically, commonly watched treasury-curve inversions have often preceded us recessions, but the lead time varies and the relationship is not a deterministic forecast.the 10y-2y vs 10y-3mthe linked new york fed model uses the ten-year minus three-month treasury yield spread to estimate a probability for a stated future horizon. the ten-year minus two-year spread is a different series. model probabilities depend on the model and sample and are not certain outcomes; the two spreads need not invert on the same date.trading around the curvethe curve is a slow-moving macro indicator. treat it as one piece of economic context rather than as an intraday timing tool or an automatic instruction to change a portfolio.(educational only — not financial advice. tradehq offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; it is one historical recession-risk indicator with uncertain timing; it predicts the exact market bottom; it only matters for day traders. correct answer: it is one historical recession-risk indicator with uncertain timing. why: yield-curve inversion is informative context, but it is not a guaranteed or precisely timed forecast.the yield curve by itself provides: options: an exact entry time; homecoursesmacro reading for tradersthe dollar index (dxy) — reading currency contextintermediate·lesson 4 of 5·7 min readthe dollar index (dxy) — reading currency contextdxy tracks the dollar against six currencies and offers context for studying currency exposure, with important limits.by anuga weerasinghepublished by tradehq, created by anuga weerasinghe. publisher background and editorial approach. no independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. quick answerthe dollar index (dxy) — reading currency context?dxy tracks the dollar against six currencies and offers context for studying currency exposure, with important limits. dxy's euro weight is 57.6%; the basket does not represent every currency. earnings effects depend on actual currency exposure, costs and hedging.what the basket measuresice's us dollar index measures the dollar against six currencies: euro (57.6%), japanese yen (13.6%), british pound (11.9%), canadian dollar (9.1%), swedish krona (4.2%) and swiss franc (3.6%). it is heavily weighted toward the euro and excludes many trading partners. a dxy rise therefore does not imply the same dollar appreciation against every currency.translation and company earningsdollar appreciation against a company's revenue currencies can reduce the dollar value of unhedged foreign earnings. the overall effect also depends on costs, hedges, pricing and the currencies involved. federal reserve research describes translation and export-competitiveness channels; it does not establish a universal conversion from a dxy percentage move to s&p 500 earnings per share.a currency worksheetsuppose a fictional company earns eur 1 million and has no hedge. at $1.10 per euro, translation gives $1.10 million; at $1.00 per euro, it gives $1.00 million. that $100,000 difference is an illustration for one currency and one unchanged earnings amount. it is not an eps forecast, and a move in dxy alone does not supply those exchange rates.commodities and other influencesfor a dollar-priced commodity with an unchanged dollar price, a weaker local currency raises the local-currency purchase cost. in actual markets, commodity prices also change with supply, demand, inventories and interest rates. an inverse relationship with the dollar can appear in a selected sample, but it is not a fixed rule for gold or any other commodity.dollar borrowing in emerging marketsa borrower with dollar debt and local-currency income can face a larger local-currency debt-service burden when that currency weakens against the dollar. dollar revenues or hedges can offset some exposure. bis research studies broader links between dollar strength and financial conditions; effects vary across economies and periods, so dxy is not an automatic equity signal.compare indicators rather than choose oneread dxy alongside relevant bilateral exchange rates, a broader trade-weighted dollar index, interest rates and the asset's own context. for a study exercise, compare the same dated observations over a chosen interval and report where relationships change. a correlation does not show that the dollar caused another asset's move or predict the next trade.(educational only — not financial advice. tradehq offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) key takeawaysdxy's euro weight is 57.6%; the basket does not represent every currency.earnings effects depend on actual currency exposure, costs and hedging.dollar and commodity relationships vary over time.dollar debt exposure depends on the borrower's income currency and hedges.check your understandinganswer all 4 questions to complete this lesson.1. largest dxy weight:yenpoundeuro (~57.6%)yuan2. dollar appreciation can reduce translated earnings when a company has:no foreign exposureunhedged foreign-currency earningsonly dollar revenue and costsno earnings3. a gold-dxy correlation measured over one period:guarantees the next price moveproves dollar moves cause gold movesmay differ in another periodis always positive4. which borrower is directly exposed to a larger local-currency burden when its currency weakens against the dollar?one with matching dollar income and debtone with unhedged dollar debt and local-currency incomeone with no debtevery borrower equallysubmit & complete lessonanswer noteslargest dxy weight: options: yen; pound; euro (~57.6%); yuan. correct answer: euro (~57.6%). why: the euro has a 57.6% weight in ice's six-currency basket.dollar appreciation can reduce translated earnings when a company has: options: no foreign exposure; unhedged foreign-currency earnings; only dollar revenue and costs; no earnings. correct answer: unhedged foreign-currency earnings. why: unchanged foreign-currency earnings translate into fewer dollars if the dollar strengthens against that currency. this is not a universal eps forecast.a gold-dxy correlation measured over one period: options: guarantees the next price move; proves dollar moves cause gold moves; may differ in another period; is always positive. correct answer: may differ in another period. why: correlation depends on the selected sample and does not establish causation or a fixed trading rule.which borrower is directly exposed to a larger local-currency burden when its currency weakens against the dollar? options: one with matching dollar income and debt; one with unhedged dollar debt and local-currency income; one with no debt; every borrower equally. correct answer: one with unhedged dollar debt and local-currency income. why: currency mismatch can increase the local-currency cost of dollar debt service; hedges or dollar revenues can change that exposure.sources & further readingice — us dollar index composition federal reserve — dollar appreciation and corporate profits (2015) bis — exchange rates and financial conditions in emes (2023) fred — broad trade-weighted us dollar index the yield curve and recession-risk researchputting it together — a macro dashboard for traders practise this lessonuse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and daily settlement are conceptual exercises: calculate their examples in a worksheet, because tradehq does not execute derivatives contracts. educational simulation only — not financial advice.macro reading for tradersall courseseducational simulation only — not financial advice. virtual money; homecoursesmacro reading for tradersthe dollar index (dxy) — reading currency contextintermediate·lesson 4 of 5·7 min readthe dollar index (dxy) — reading currency contextdxy tracks the dollar against six currencies and offers context for studying currency exposure, with important limits.by anuga weerasinghepublished by tradehq, created by anuga weerasinghe. publisher background and editorial approach. no independent professional review is claimed; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page. quick answerthe dollar index (dxy) — reading currency context?dxy tracks the dollar against six currencies and offers context for studying currency exposure, with important limits. dxy's euro weight is 57.6%; the basket does not represent every currency. earnings effects depend on actual currency exposure, costs and hedging.what the basket measuresice's us dollar index measures the dollar against six currencies: euro (57.6%), japanese yen (13.6%), british pound (11.9%), canadian dollar (9.1%), swedish krona (4.2%) and swiss franc (3.6%). it is heavily weighted toward the euro and excludes many trading partners. a dxy rise therefore does not imply the same dollar appreciation against every currency.translation and company earningsdollar appreciation against a company's revenue currencies can reduce the dollar value of unhedged foreign earnings. the overall effect also depends on costs, hedges, pricing and the currencies involved. federal reserve research describes translation and export-competitiveness channels; it does not establish a universal conversion from a dxy percentage move to s&p 500 earnings per share.a currency worksheetsuppose a fictional company earns eur 1 million and has no hedge. at $1.10 per euro, translation gives $1.10 million; at $1.00 per euro, it gives $1.00 million. that $100,000 difference is an illustration for one currency and one unchanged earnings amount. it is not an eps forecast, and a move in dxy alone does not supply those exchange rates.commodities and other influencesfor a dollar-priced commodity with an unchanged dollar price, a weaker local currency raises the local-currency purchase cost. in actual markets, commodity prices also change with supply, demand, inventories and interest rates. an inverse relationship with the dollar can appear in a selected sample, but it is not a fixed rule for gold or any other commodity.dollar borrowing in emerging marketsa borrower with dollar debt and local-currency income can face a larger local-currency debt-service burden when that currency weakens against the dollar. dollar revenues or hedges can offset some exposure. bis research studies broader links between dollar strength and financial conditions; effects vary across economies and periods, so dxy is not an automatic equity signal.compare indicators rather than choose oneread dxy alongside relevant bilateral exchange rates, a broader trade-weighted dollar index, interest rates and the asset's own context. for a study exercise, compare the same dated observations over a chosen interval and report where relationships change. a correlation does not show that the dollar caused another asset's move or predict the next trade.(educational only — not financial advice. tradehq offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) key takeawaysdxy's euro weight is 57.6%; the basket does not represent every currency.earnings effects depend on actual currency exposure, costs and hedging.dollar and commodity relationships vary over time.dollar debt exposure depends on the borrower's income currency and hedges.check your understandinganswer all 4 questions to complete this lesson.1. largest dxy weight:yenpoundeuro (~57.6%)yuan2. dollar appreciation can reduce translated earnings when a company has:no foreign exposureunhedged foreign-currency earningsonly dollar revenue and costsno earnings3. a gold-dxy correlation measured over one period:guarantees the next price moveproves dollar moves cause gold movesmay differ in another periodis always positive4. which borrower is directly exposed to a larger local-currency burden when its currency weakens against the dollar?one with matching dollar income and debtone with unhedged dollar debt and local-currency incomeone with no debtevery borrower equallysubmit & complete lessonanswer noteslargest dxy weight: options: yen; pound; euro (~57.6%); yuan. correct answer: euro (~57.6%). why: the euro has a 57.6% weight in ice's six-currency basket.dollar appreciation can reduce translated earnings when a company has: options: no foreign exposure; unhedged foreign-currency earnings; only dollar revenue and costs; no earnings. correct answer: unhedged foreign-currency earnings. why: unchanged foreign-currency earnings translate into fewer dollars if the dollar strengthens against that currency. this is not a universal eps forecast.a gold-dxy correlation measured over one period: options: guarantees the next price move; proves dollar moves cause gold moves; may differ in another period; is always positive. correct answer: may differ in another period. why: correlation depends on the selected sample and does not establish causation or a fixed trading rule.which borrower is directly exposed to a larger local-currency burden when its currency weakens against the dollar? options: one with matching dollar income and debt; this lesson does not rank causes of trading losses.what tilt actually istilt describes an emotional reaction to recent outcomes that can pull decisions away from a plan. after a loss, a trader may feel pressure to recover it immediately. that is a prompt for reflection, not evidence that the next trade will win or lose. this lesson uses hypothetical situations and does not rank the causes of account losses.notice the urge to change the plana useful practice question is whether the next decision follows the original plan or is mainly a response to the last result. write down any urge to increase size, re-enter immediately or abandon the original rationale. these observations are personal journal notes, not a diagnosis or a reliable prediction of performance.the revenge trade patterna hypothetical sequence is loss, frustration, an unplanned increase in position size and another loss. the eventual drawdown depends on the positions and price changes; no particular percentage follows automatically from that sequence. in a practice journal, compare the intended position size with the size actually submitted.concrete circuit breakersa practice plan can include a chosen daily loss threshold and a pause to review decisions. for arithmetic only, 3% of a hypothetical $100,000 starting balance is $3,000; the holding has a $200 gross marked value at that price. a later displayed price of $105 would value the 2 units at $210 and show a $10 gross price change. a later hypothetical sale would have additional fees. the exercise is about distinguishing gross and net arithmetic, not a claim about an asset.fields worth recordingpossible fields include date and timezone, ticker and instrument type, quantity, observed source and quote age, virtual order price, transaction fee, original question, alternative explanation, and planned review criterion. more columns are not automatically better; use only what serves the learning question.review observations, not imagined causesgrouping past results may reveal a calculation error or a difference between chosen samples. it does not establish that the labels in a journal caused those outcomes. record unfavorable cases and changes in rules, and avoid interpreting a convenient short sample as proof of a repeatable method.sample-size limitsno fixed number such as 30 or 100 decisions proves reliability. market conditions and dependence between observations matter, as do selection bias, virtual fill assumptions and transaction costs. a journal supports transparent accounting; it does not license larger real-money positions.(educational only — not financial advice. tradehq offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; favorable and unfavorable cases under recorded rules. correct answer: favorable and unfavorable cases under recorded rules. why: selecting only attractive cases makes the summary misleading.does 30 recorded trades establish a reliable strategy? options: no universal sample count can do that; any recorded source-check scope appears on the page.source check: 2026-10-18. checked arithmetic and removed unsupported physical-health and professional-behaviour claims. quick answerunderstanding drawdowns in a simulation?calculate declines from a previous portfolio peak and compare hypothetical sizing and recovery assumptions. drawdown is measured from a previous peak, with a clear valuation basis. recovering from a decline requires calculating the gain on the reduced base.what drawdown actually measuresa drawdown compares a portfolio's value with an earlier peak, using the same measurement basis. if an illustrative virtual portfolio peaks at $100,000 and later marks at $90,000, the peak-to-trough drawdown is ($100,000 - $90,000) / $100,000 = 10%. this number describes a past decline, not the probability of a future loss.a different denominator for recoverymoving from $90,000 back to $100,000 requires $10,000 / $90,000, or approximately 11.11% growth, not 10%. a 20% decline from $100,000 to $80,000 requires a 25% gain to return to the same previous peak. this asymmetry is simple arithmetic; it does not prescribe a trading strategy.the effect of sizing assumptionsthe same assumed asset movement can produce different portfolio-level changes depending on allocation. in a fee-free illustration, a 20% drop in an asset that is 10% of a $100,000 portfolio contributes approximately a 2% portfolio decline if everything else stays constant. concentration, other holdings, fees and timing can change the observed result.sequence and measurement matterdrawdown depends on the path of account values, not only the first and final price. specify whether account values include fees, deposits or withdrawals, and whether valuations are current or delayed. a sequence built from generated practice candles is not an observed market drawdown.testing changes to a fictional rulea learner may compare two explicitly hypothetical size schedules after a recorded decline. define each rule before looking at its result; document any change so a revised rule is not mixed with the original sample. no fixed 10%, 20% or other threshold is universally suitable.scope of this lessona portfolio decline cannot be used to diagnose stress, sleep, hormones or mental-health conditions. this lesson teaches virtual portfolio arithmetic and uncertainty, not healthcare guidance or advice about recovering real financial losses.(educational only — not financial advice. tradehq offers $100,000 virtual cash for supported spot instruments. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and settlement are conceptual exercises; the simulator does not execute them.) key takeawaysdrawdown is measured from a previous peak, with a clear valuation basis.recovering from a decline requires calculating the gain on the reduced base.allocation, costs and price sequence affect portfolio-level outcomes.no particular drawdown threshold or response is universally validated.check your understandinganswer all 4 questions to complete this lesson.1. a virtual portfolio falls from $100,000 to $90,000. its peak-to-trough drawdown is:5%10%11.11%90%2. how much growth returns $90,000 to $100,000?10%1%20%about 11.11%3. what determines portfolio impact from an asset loss?allocation and the asset's movement, among other factorsonly the tickeronly the price per unitthe lesson completion badge4. can a drawdown percentage diagnose a health condition?yesonly after 30 tradesnoonly for experienced traderssubmit & complete lessonanswer notesa virtual portfolio falls from $100,000 to $90,000. its peak-to-trough drawdown is: options: 5%; 10%; 11.11%; 90%. correct answer: 10%. why: $10,000 divided by the $100,000 peak is 10%.how much growth returns $90,000 to $100,000? options: 10%; 1%; 20%; about 11.11%. correct answer: about 11.11%. why: the $10,000 recovery is divided by the lower $90,000 balance.what determines portfolio impact from an asset loss? options: allocation and the asset's movement, among other factors; only the ticker; only the price per unit; the lesson completion badge. correct answer: allocation and the asset's movement, among other factors. why: position weight affects the portfolio-level change.can a drawdown percentage diagnose a health condition? options: yes; only after 30 trades; no; only for experienced traders. correct answer: no. why: a finance calculation is not a medical assessment.sources & further readingsec investor.gov — risk sec investor.gov — past-performance limitations optional checklists for practice sessionsback to track practise this lessonuse $100,000 in virtual cash to practise supported spot instruments and general habits such as recording a trade thesis. options contracts, greeks, futures margin and daily settlement are conceptual exercises: calculate their examples in a worksheet, because tradehq does not execute derivatives contracts. educational simulation only — not financial advice.trading decisions and behaviourall courseseducational simulation only — not financial advice. virtual money;
